summary:
On a mountain, every point before the top is followed by a higher point and every point from the top onward
by a lower one. Comparing `e[mid]` with `e[mid + 1]` tells you which side of the top mid is on, so binary
search finds the top in O(log n).

question.md:
Elevations rise strictly to one top and then fall strictly; the top is never at either end. Return its index
in O(log n).

- **Strictly** rising and falling: no flat stretches, so "next is higher" is a clean yes/no.
- **Exactly one top**, never at index 0 or n − 1.

think.md:
Take `[1, 4, 6, 9, 13, 11, 7, 2]`. Ask, for each point, "is the next point higher?": yes, yes, yes, yes, then no from the top
onwards.

think.caption: The answers flip from yes to no exactly at the top.

think.md:
A yes/no question that flips once is exactly what binary search finds. At `mid`: if `e[mid] < e[mid + 1]`
we're on the way up, so the top is to the right (`lo = mid + 1`); otherwise we're at the top or past it
(`hi = mid`). Using `mid + 1` is always safe because `mid < hi ≤ n − 1`.

approaches.title: Walk up until it falls

idea.md: Return the first index whose next point is lower.

build: For i from 0: if `e[i] > e[i + 1]`, return i.

lines.text: Climb while the next point is higher. The top is never the last point, so `i + 1` stays in range.
The first point followed by a lower one.

steps.text: 13 > 11: the trail starts falling, so index 4 is the top.

walk.title: Walk up the trail until the next point is lower.

limits.md: Climbs one step at a time; the required O(log n) needs halving.

approaches.title: Binary search on the slope

idea.md: `lo = 0`, `hi = n − 1`. While `lo < hi`: if `e[mid] < e[mid + 1]`, `lo = mid + 1`; else `hi = mid`. Return `lo`.

build: Compare mid with its right neighbour and keep the half containing the top.

lines.text: The top is somewhere in [0, n − 1].
`mid < hi`, so `mid + 1` is a valid index.
Rising after mid: the top is further right. Falling: mid is the top or past it, so keep mid.
The single remaining index is the top.

steps.text: lo=0, hi=7, mid=3: 9 < 13, so the trail rises after mid: a summit lies to the right, lo = 4.
lo=4, hi=7, mid=5: 11 > 7, so the trail falls after mid: a summit lies at mid or to its left, hi = 5.
lo=4, hi=5, mid=4: 13 > 11, so the trail falls after mid: a summit lies at mid or to its left, hi = 4.

walk.title: Look at the slope at mid: rising means the top is to the right, falling means it's at mid or to the left.

takeaways.md:
- Binary search doesn't need sorted data, only a yes/no question that flips once: "is the next point
  higher?"
- Compare `a[mid]` with `a[mid + 1]` and keep the side that contains the peak.
